messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 54
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Chef
  trauma_type: Assault
  pcl5: 68

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Certain Conversation Topics: Certain conversation topics, Emotional Closeness: Someone getting emotionally close to me, Male Presence: Being alone with men
  Threat: Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Threat from Strangers: I feel threatened by strangers approaching me even in ordinary situations, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Fragmented Pieces: My memories of the event come in disconnected pieces that do not fit together, Bodily Reenactment: When memories come to mind of what happened, I feel my body is in the same position as when the frightening event occurred.
  Negative Appraisals: Fear of Harm: You can never know who will harm you, Betrayal: I was betrayed by someone I trusted, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Clinical Vignette: Margot

Margot is a fifty-four-year-old chef of Polish descent who was assaulted in her restaurant's walk-in freezer eight months ago by a delivery driver she had worked with for nearly three years. She had known him by name, had made small talk with him on dozens of occasions, had trusted him enough to unlock the freezer when he arrived with a late shipment. What happened inside that space—the sudden violence, the way his hands moved, the temperature that made everything feel unreal—she cannot yet assemble into a coherent narrative. When she tries to speak about it in therapy, words scatter. She describes instead the sensation of her spine pressed against cold metal shelving, the particular quality of the fluorescent light, the smell of frozen meat and her own fear. The event exists in her body more completely than it exists in language.

Since that evening, Margot has reorganized her life around the conviction that trust is a dangerous mistake. The man who hurt her had worn a familiar uniform, had greeted her by her first name, had given no warning. She had come to believe that you cannot know who will harm you—that the appearance of ordinariness is itself a mask. When strangers approach her now, even in the grocery store or on the street, her body tightens as though danger is certain. She monitors the distance between herself and unfamiliar men with an intensity that exhausts her. In her kitchen, where she once moved with fluid confidence, she now startles violently at any unexpected movement—a sous chef reaching past her, a delivery person appearing around a corner. The startle is not small or manageable; it is a full-body recoil, a moment in which she experiences the movement as threat.

Her marriage has become strained in ways that puzzle her husband, Michael. He cannot understand why she flinches when he approaches her from behind, or why certain conversations—ones in which he tries to discuss what happened, or in which she senses he is trying to draw her into emotional intimacy—cause her to withdraw or become sharp with him. She has come to dread being alone with him, though she cannot fully articulate why. He is not the man who hurt her. Yet the simple fact of his maleness, of his physical presence when there is no one else nearby, generates a vigilance in her that feels both protective and imprisoning. She locks the bathroom door when she showers. She sleeps facing the door.

The restaurant has suffered. Margot has always been the kind of chef who worked the line herself, who moved through her kitchen as its vital center. Now she has hired an assistant manager and spends more time in the office, away from the floor. This decision was framed as a promotion, but it is actually retreat. She cannot manage the unpredictability of the kitchen environment anymore—the constant movement of bodies, the necessary trust in her team, the vulnerability of being watched while she works. Two of her longest-serving cooks have asked for transfers. She knows they sense her distance, her hypervigilance, the way she has become someone other than the woman who taught them.

What brought Margot to seek help now, after eight months of managing alone, was a moment last week when Michael tried to hold her hand during dinner and she experienced a surge of panic so acute that she stood up from the table and locked herself in the bedroom. She sat on the edge of the bed feeling the phantom pressure of that freezer wall against her back, feeling her body in that old position, and she understood that the life she is living—cordoned off, vigilant, unable to be touched by the one person who loves her—has become another kind of trap. She is terrified that therapy will ask her to trust again, and equally terrified that she will spend the rest of her life unable to do so.
